lesson.title: Combining True and False: and, or, not
lesson.summary: Logical operators and, or, and not combine or invert boolean expressions, letting a program test several conditions at once instead of just one.
lesson.body:
A single comparison can only test one relationship at a time: is age at least 13, is the password correct, is the list empty. Real decisions are rarely that narrow. Whether someone qualifies for a discount might depend on being a member and having a coupon. Whether a login attempt should be blocked might depend on the password being wrong or the account being locked. Python provides exactly three logical operators for building these compound conditions out of simpler boolean expressions: and, or, and not. Each one takes existing boolean expressions, the same kind produced by comparisons like == or <, and produces a new boolean expression as its result.

and combines two boolean expressions and evaluates to True only when both sides are True. or combines two boolean expressions and evaluates to True when at least one side is True. not is different from the other two because it only takes a single boolean expression and flips it: True becomes False, and False becomes True. The next three sections walk through each of these operators individually and in depth, including a few behaviors, like short circuit evaluation, that are easy to miss on a first read.

A short trace shows how naturally these fit together with comparisons already covered in this chapter:

temperature = 72
is_sunny = True
good_for_picnic = temperature > 65 and is_sunny
print(good_for_picnic)

Python first evaluates temperature > 65, substituting 72 for temperature, which gives True. is_sunny is already a boolean variable holding True. The and operator then combines True and True, producing True, which is what good_for_picnic ends up holding.

One detail worth knowing early is precedence: when an expression mixes not, and, and or without parentheses, Python evaluates not first, then and, then or, similar to how multiplication happens before addition in arithmetic. Because that ordering is not always obvious to a reader, many programmers add parentheses even when they are not strictly required, purely to make the intended grouping unmistakable. Mastering these three operators is what separates programs that can only ask one question at a time from programs that can weigh several conditions together, which is close to the heart of what makes conditional logic powerful.

Parentheses become especially important once and, or, and not appear together in the same expression. Consider access = (is_admin or is_owner) and not is_banned. With is_admin set to False, is_owner set to True, and is_banned set to True, Python first evaluates the parenthesized part: False or True evaluates to True. It then evaluates not is_banned, which flips True to False. Finally, and combines True and False, giving False overall, so access is denied because of the ban, even though the user qualifies as an owner. Dropping the parentheses and writing is_admin or is_owner and not is_banned would evaluate differently, because Python's precedence rules apply not first, then and, then or, grouping the expression as is_admin or (is_owner and not is_banned) instead. For these particular values that happens to still produce False, but the two expressions are not equivalent in general, which is exactly why relying on memorized precedence rather than explicit parentheses is a common source of subtle bugs.
